why_angle: The SoundGuys roundup that the shopper's sources cite says the Arctis Nova 5X connects to Xbox. It never says that the look-alike Nova 5 and Nova 5P cannot, not even with a 5X dongle. It also skips the dongle's switch positions and Microsoft's rule on which headsets Series X|S accepts. This page takes all three from SteelSeries' and Microsoft's own pages and sets them out for each candidate, platform by platform.

page.answer: Short answer. For one gaming headset across PC, PS5 and Xbox, get the SteelSeries Arctis Nova 5X. Xbox compatibility is built into the headset, not the dongle: a Nova 5 or 5P won't work on Xbox, even with a 5X dongle. Wired, the HyperX Cloud III covers PC, PlayStation, Xbox and Switch.

page.after:
What the differences mean

  • Arctis Nova 5X battery on the dongle: SoundGuys measured 42 h 10 min. SteelSeries rates the 2.4 GHz link at 50 h (as quoted by SoundGuys), so 42.17 ÷ 50 = 84% of the rating. At 3 hours of play a day that is 42 ÷ 3 = 14 days between charges, not the 60 ÷ 3 = 20 days the 60-hour headline suggests (that figure is the Bluetooth rating).
  • Logitech PRO X 2 battery: SoundGuys measured 88 h 27 min against Logitech's 50 h claim, so 88.45 ÷ 50 = 177%. SoundGuys ran it at 75 dB but ran the Nova 5X at about 50% volume, so the two results are not a like-for-like ranking.
  • HyperX Cloud III S Wireless battery: 120 h rated on 2.4 GHz ÷ 3 h a day = 40 days. 120 ÷ 42 = 2.9× the Nova 5X's measured figure, but that compares a rating with a measurement and the S Wireless is not listed for Xbox.
  • Wired prices: the HyperX Cloud III Wired at $57.99 costs $59.99 − $57.99 = $2.00 less than the Razer BlackShark V2 X. The EKSA E900 Pro costs $57.99 − $46.99 = $11.00 less than the Cloud III. The EKSA Fenrir S is $36.99.
  • PRO X 2 on Xbox: on Xbox it plugs in by 3.5 mm cable, so on that console you are paying $219.99 for a wired headset.

Why Xbox support has to be in the headset you buy

Microsoft's rule for Xbox Series X|S covers two routes. USB works only for an "officially licensed" accessory. The 3.5 mm jack on the Xbox Wireless Controller takes "any headset". A generic wireless dongle does not make a headset an Xbox headset. That is why one SteelSeries model works on Xbox and its near-twins do not.

  • Only the 5X: SteelSeries Support says "The Arctis Nova 5X is the only Nova 5 model built for Xbox". It adds that the Nova 5 and Nova 5P "won't work with Xbox—even if you'd purchase the Nova 5X dongle separately." The X has to be on the box when you buy. You cannot add it later.
  • Set the switch: the Nova 5X dongle has two positions. Use Xbox for an Xbox Series X|S or Xbox One, and USB for a PC, a PlayStation or other platforms. If the headset will not connect on Xbox, check this switch first.
  • The same split at HyperX: HyperX lists the Cloud III Wired for Xbox Series X|S and Xbox One. Its own listing for the Cloud III Wireless names only PC, PS5 and Nintendo Switch.
  • Logitech PRO X 2: Logitech's US product page names no consoles. SoundGuys used its dongle on PC, PS5 and a docked Switch, and on an Xbox Series X connected it with the 3.5 mm cable. The reviewer measured 200–250 ms of delay over Bluetooth and called that too slow for competitive play.
  • Surround claims on consoles: Razer says the BlackShark V2 X's 7.1 surround is "Only available on Windows 11". Over 3.5 mm on a console you get stereo.

Not recommended

The Arctis Nova 5 or Nova 5P, if there is or may be an Xbox in the house. They look like the 5X and sit next to it in store listings, but SteelSeries says neither will ever work with Xbox, even with a 5X dongle. If you can't see "5X" or "Xbox" in the product name, pick another listing.
